title: Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy
description: US President Donald Trump says he has created a new task force focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intellige
body: US President Donald Trump says he has created a new task force focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday.Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael will also be part of the task force.Trump said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact to regulate the technology."The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote.He also named Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor as a member of the taskforce, which will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.The announcement follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public."The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves.The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google.

schema.headline: Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy

title: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country
description: Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to
body: Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel.The co-pilot is alleged to have attacked the captain with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers managed to overpower him and successfully take control of the plane.The Australian authorities have not identified the co-pilot, who has been named by multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times as Hamam al-Hammami.The prosecutor in the UAE has said it is investigating the incident and any possible motives.In a statement to the BBC, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed its investigation into "the man's links to Australia".The investigation involves state police and the country's security agency, it said, adding that an update would be "provided at the appropriate time".Sources familiar with the case, who have spoken to Australian media, have said the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014, and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, until he left the country.The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) said the co-pilot's student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was no longer enrolled in a course, making him ineligible for it.Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he was an Omani national. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September was carrying more than 170 passengers to Israel. Two and a half hours into its journey, the plane plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) when the Omani co-pilot attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.The pilot flying the plane, Capt Smit Machchhar, described how he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.Machchhar, an Indian national, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.The co-pilot was arrested after the emergency landing and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu.The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said on Saturday investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.He said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.In the days since the attack more details have come to light about the co-pilot's employment history.While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.It is also known that, from 2020, he was studying on a distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK.He graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

schema.headline: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country

title: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues
description: The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.The measu
body: The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.The measures include plans for longer opening hours, as well as an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.A museum spokesperson said the public response to the 11th Century embroidery had been "extraordinary", but acknowledged that some visitors had waited longer than they would have wanted.Some people reported waits of up to two hours, while hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early last week due to a private event.Some ticket holders took to social media to complain about the disruption. One disappointed visitor said the trip had been a "big event" they had looked forward to, while another wrote she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux Tapestry, and bought tickets only to be turned away after queuing.The museum later apologised to those who had been unable to enter and said they would be issued refunds and priority booking slots for a rearranged time.From Monday, visitors will be offered an audio guide with more information about the embroidery, while additional signage and seating will be provided for those queuing to reach the main exhibition.The museum said it planned to introduce longer opening hours to prevent queues building during the day and allow people with later bookings more time to view the exhibition. Details of the extended hours have not yet been disclosed.Demand for the exhibition has been high since tickets first went on sale in July, with a record 100,000 sold on the first day. Members of the public who were not successful in the first ticket release will have two further chances to view the masterpiece when further tickets go on sale in October and January. Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared with its usual €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy. Children under 16 can visit the London exhibition for free. The exhibition opened on 10 September but has experienced a series of problems with queues and congestion, with some visitors spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry.Visitors were later stopped from taking photographs and a recorded message was introduced encouraging people to continue moving through the one-way exhibition.The 70m-long Bayeux Tapestry depicts 58 scenes outlining the extraordinary events surrounding the Norman conquest of England, the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and the end of Anglo-Saxon rule in Britain.Despite its name, the work is an embroidery rather than a tapestry and contains approximately 626 human figures and 200 horses.The Bayeux Tapestry is on loan from the French government, having been transported from its home in Normandy - where it has been exhibited since 1983. It will be on display until July 2027.The loan marks the first time the tapestry has returned to the UK since it was created more than 900 years ago.

schema.headline: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues

title: Daughter of murdered MP Sir David Amess says politicians still at risk
description: The review is being led by former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland, with the aim of reporting within six months.The safety of politi
body: The review is being led by former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland, with the aim of reporting within six months.The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years since the death of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe in July this year, Sir David's murder in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox's murder in 2016.The five years since her father was killed have been "absolutely devastating and heartbreaking", his daughter told Kuenssberg, adding: "It's a very, very real situation that we're living with."She has previously called for a public inquiry into the safety of politicians so people can have "the full facts to hand, full openness, honesty, and transparency".The nearing anniversary of Sir David's murder comes after the man accused of murdering Widdecombe was also charged with preparing acts of terror, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Amess, who knew Widdecombe as a family friend and called her Aunt Ann, said: "It's absolutely so tragic and heartbreaking that now she isn't here either." She added: "My dad was murdered five years ago so if so much has changed why are we still seeing other members of parliament or former members of parliament being targeted like this."Widdecombe was not a sitting member of parliament when she died, but was a member of the Conservative Party and the member for Maidstone and the Weald from 1987 to 2010. She became a member of Reform UK in 2019.Separately, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch confirmed to the BBC the man who pleaded guilty to sending her threatening messages also sent them to her family.Kieran Kyle, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature to Badenoch and her family when he appeared in court in September. He will be sentenced on October 29."I just think that whether it's Nigel Farage, or even Keir Starmer who had his home fire bombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this,"  she told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.Asked how Badenoch coped with threats to her safety, she replied: "it's really tough, but you just have to get on with it".Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told the BBC he also experienced threats to his safety, told the programme "this was far from where any of us want to be"."We have to find the middle ground where we're accessible but we're protected and in the overall scheme of things if that requires a bit of extra taxpayers' money, I think hopefully voters would say 'yes'."Amess said her father "loved meeting people", saying "he was one of the easier members of parliament to take a meeting with because that's what he lived for - to meet people, shake their hands, smile, help them with their problems. My dad wouldn't have wanted constituency surgeries to stop."She added that he would have wanted to be alerted to someone being reported as a potential threat.His killer, Ali Harbi Ali had been referred to the government's counter-terror programme Prevent in October 2014 but his case was closed in 2016.A review published in February 2025 found Ali's Prevent case was closed too early after "problematic" assessments.

schema.headline: Daughter of murdered MP Sir David Amess says politicians still at risk

title: WRC: Elfyn Evans becomes world champion after late Oliver Solberg crash
description: Evans ends Britain's 25-year wait for WRC championImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Elfyn Evans and co-driver Scott Martin won just two of 13 r
body: Evans ends Britain's 25-year wait for WRC championImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Elfyn Evans and co-driver Scott Martin won just two of 13 races in the 2026 WRC seasonElfyn Evans became Britain's first world rally champion for 25 years after rival Oliver Solberg crashed in a highly dramatic finish to the season in Italy.Sweden's Solberg was on course to snatch the lead on the final stage of the last round of the World Rally Championship, and thereby deny Evans the title.But Solberg lost control of his car with a few hundred metres to go in the Rally Italia Sardegna, which meant the glory went to Welshman Evans, a five-time runner-up in the championship."It hasn't sunk in," said a shocked Evans."I was sure it was over. I feel for Oliver - he had an incredible weekend. I don't know what to say."The 37-year-old and co-driver Scott Martin had led for much of the 2026 season and took a 21-point advantage into the final round in Sardinia.But that gap had shrunk to a solitary point by the time the drivers lined up for the last of 17 stages, bringing back painful memories of previous narrow misses for Evans.Solberg, 25, needed only to beat his Toyota team-mate in the final stage to claim enough bonuses to be champion, but he crashed two corners from the finish.Evans becomes only the third British man to win the WRC title after Colin McRae in 1995 and Richard Burns in 2001.Figure caption, World champion Evans reflects on 'incredible finish'Solberg, whose father Petter won the WRC title in 2003, won the rally by almost a minute ahead of nine-time world champion Sebastien Ogier.With barely a kilometre to run of the final stage he and English co-driver Elliott Edmondson were 1.9 seconds up on Evans and closing at speed on the championship.Though Solberg got back on the road, his crash meant he finished nine seconds slower than his team-mate - and five points behind Evans in the overall standings.A third Toyota driver, Sami Pajari, finished a further one point behind in third - having seen his own title challenge evaporate on the final weekend.An inconsolable Solberg remained in his car for some time at the end of the stage before being encouraged to take to the podium by Gazoo Racing team principal Jari-Matti Latvala and team-mate Ogier."Two corners, two corners," said an emotional Solberg."First congratulations to Elfyn, he has been very consistent all season. That I even had a shot after my rollercoaster of a season is incredible."I tried everything. I knew I was pushing but didn't know if it was enough. I pushed even more and I couldn't save the car. I tried my very best."Evans, from Dolgellau in north Wales, had previously missed out on the title on the final day three times and in two of those seasons he had taken a lead into the concluding rally before losing out to Ogier in 2020 and 2025."I don't really know what my reaction is. It's surreal with how it happened. It's a relief," he said."It wouldn't by my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done."For Toyota sporting director Kaj Lindstrom there were mixed feelings."That was the hardest thing. The ending was quite something, I didn't expect it," said the Finn."It was a good fight and we all saw that Oliver was all or nothing. It held all the way to the end."Oliver still has time but Elfyn finally got his title so we're really happy for him."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jon Armstrong was competing in his first full season at the top level in the World Rally ChampionshipThe WRC season was reduced to 13 rounds when the Saudi Arabia event, originally planned for next month, was cancelled because of the ongoing unrest in the Middle East.Rally Italia Sardegna marked the end of Jon Armstrong's rookie season at the top level of WRC, and he produced his best result when finishing seventh."It's been good to have a clean weekend with a strong result," said the M-Sport Ford driver."It's not been an easy year and this was a rally to show we can put it together. A big thanks to everyone who has been supporting us, it's been a great year and it's been a privilege to drive this car."Armstrong's team-mate and fellow Irishman Josh McErlean did not fare as well despite running as high as sixth on Saturday before retiring after a collision with a tree.He also had to stop twice on Sunday before finishing well off the pace but claimed ninth spot in the championship.Rally Italia Sardegna result1. title: The sexual abuse of disabled residents that shocked South Korea
description: ⁠⁠Forced to call him 'Dad': The trial over sexual abuse in a disabled care home that has shocked South KoreaImage source, Getty ImagesByJuna MoonBBC K
body: ⁠⁠Forced to call him 'Dad': The trial over sexual abuse in a disabled care home that has shocked South KoreaImage source, Getty ImagesByJuna MoonBBC Korean"I was hurting inside, so I came to tell my story."These were Seo Mi-hyeon's first words to the police.Seo, who has an intellectual disability, struggles to form long sentences and can only communicate through brief words and gestures. But her memories of the abuse inflicted upon her were clear.She was one of three residents at a state-run care home in South Korea who were sexually assaulted by the home's director, in a case that has shocked the country and raised serious questions about state care for the disabled.Earlier this month, a court in Seoul sentenced the director - who has only been identified by his surname Kim - to 15 years in prison. Kim is appealing the conviction.The court had heard that some residents were made to call the director "Dad", which prosecutors said illustrated the unequal relationship between Kim and those in his care.The ruling came nearly two years after Seo, who is in her 40s, first disclosed the abuse to her mother. We have changed Seo's name and the names of another victim in this story to protect their identities.'I just endured it'Seo first began living in Saekdongwon, a care home for the intellectually disabled, in 2016.The institute, located in the city of Incheon, is fully subsidised by the state and still houses some 33 residents, although it has been asked to close down in light of this case. According to Seo, the abuse began shortly after she began living there, with Kim visiting her at night or in the early hours of the morning to rape her.Speaking through her lawyer Ko Eun-young, Seo said there was no adult at the facility she could speak to about the abuse, adding that she felt that other staff members would not help her. The care home has not responded to this allegation.That was her life for almost 10 years, until the case came to light in February 2025, when Seo suffered a head injury.She said it happened one of the times Kim tried to sexually assault her. She had blocked him with her hands, causing him to throw a glass at her. Her lawyer told the court that the care home took Seo to hospital and informed her mother about the incident only after the wound on her head had been stitched up.According to Seo's lawyer, Seo's mother had asked to see CCTV footage to establish how her daughter had been injured, but the facility refused, saying they were not authorised to release it.As a result, her mother brought her home and decided to withdraw her from the facility. It was only after Seo was told that she would not have to return to the home that she disclosed the sexual abuse to her mum, who then reported it to the police."I thought it was safe to speak because I was told I didn't have to go back to Saekdongwon," Seo told the BBC via her lawyer.When asked how she had managed on her own for so many years, she said: "I just endured it."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The care home was located in the Korean city of Incheon A police investigation into Seo's account was then widened to other residents.They found at least two other alleged victims, including Lee Mi-Na, who said that she was also raped by Kim.Earlier this month, a judge found all three victims' testimony credible. He was sentenced to 15 years in jail for raping Lee and Seo, five years less than the original sentence prosecutors were asking for. He has denied all allegations and has since appealed the ruling.For the third victim, Kim was found guilty of a lesser charge of sexual violence, with the judge saying the charge of rape against her was dropped as they could not find conclusive evidence that "force or threats [were used] that rendered the victim unable to resist".A joint response committee made up of disability rights and other civic groups have criticsed this ruling, saying a victim's ability to resist an assault should not impact the verdict they receive.The committee has also criticised the investigation process, saying there was a failure to identify more potential victims.In November last year, following the initial allegations of abuse, local authorities from Ganghwa County had commissioned a team from Woosuk University to conduct an in-depth assessment of Saekdongwon's residents.The report, which was submitted to the court as evidence, found indications that many more residents - at least 10 - could have been sexually assaulted by Kim.But during the trial, the court did not address this finding.According to local media reports, police had struggled to establish details of alleged abuse when interviewing residents, because most of them had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating. Some residents reportedly gave answers unrelated to the questions or did not respond at all.Image source, SADD TVImage caption, Saekdongwon was asked to close down in light of this caseKim has not responded to allegations that he may have abused more residents.Jeon Ji-su, the professor who led the Woosuk research team, told the BBC that investigators had accepted "only the accounts of people who could describe the abuse in complete sentences".But activists said that this reliance on verbal testimony meant the police failed to recognise residents with greater communication difficulties as victims."If victims express their experiences differently from the way we expect, shouldn't the state make a greater effort to hear their voices?" said Baek In-seong, of Hansahoe, a counselling centre for survivors of sexual violence with disabilities.Police have said that "while there may have been shortcomings in individual instances, these should not be taken as representative of the investigation as a whole".Rights groups have also criticised others who have sought leniency for Kim.Ahead of the verdict, a total of 13 petitions seeking leniency were said to have been submitted to the court. One of them, from a social welfare organisation, asked the court to take into account the defendant's "contribution to the welfare sector".Welfare advocacy group Gyeol condemned the petitioning organisations, saying: "Past service in the welfare sector does not exempt anyone from accountability."The judge's ruling on Kim's conviction stated that his offence was "particularly reprehensible" because "despite his professional duty to protect and support [the victims'] rights and interests and prevent abuse, he exploited the imbalance of power" with his victims to "gratify his own sexual desires".Public scrutiny and protestsThe case has shocked many in South Korea and raised questions about why the abuse was not prevented in the first place. More shocking is that it happened despite a move in 2011 to strengthen laws to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.That was the year a fictional film called Dogani, based on a true story of sexual abuse at a school for deaf children, premiered. Amid intense public scrutiny and protests, the school in question was shut and tougher laws were passed as a result.These included more specific categories of sexual offences against disabled people, harsher penalties for offences committed by facility directors and employees, and the removal of the statute of limitations for some rape offences involving disabled victims.But in the case of Saekdongwon, the abuse persisted despite regular regular inspections by Ganghwa County, the local authority responsible for overseeing the facility.A county official told the BBC that such inspections focused largely on paperwork, and that residents were interviewed only when specific issues arose. The official said there had also been an external monitoring team but it had received no reports from staff, and expressed regret that the authorities had not examined the situation more closely.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Some residents had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicatingJo Ha, a representative from the national council of a counselling centre who has supported some Saekdongwon victims, said some families she had spoken to had suspected there was abuse but felt unable to raise their concerns. Leaving a facility would mean the family has to take on all care responsibilities, as finding alternative placements is difficult.One survey conducted through a national association of parents of people living in residential facilities for those with disabilities found that around six in 10 people who secured a place in a residential facility had waited at least three years, highlighting the difficulty of accessing appropriate care.Professor Kim Yoon-tae, the head of Woosuk University's Institute of Cognitive Science, points out that such facilities exercise great control over residents' actions, from what they eat to where they sleep in addition to their access to healthcare and even whether or not to grant they could go outside.And while Saekdongwon is "a landmark case" because of the scale and duration of the abuse, it is also not an isolated incident, added Jo.In 2023, an appeals court upheld an eight-year prison sentence for a worker who raped or sexually assaulted two women with intellectual disabilities at a facility in Yeongcheon the previous year. In a separate case in Anseong, a care home worker was recently sentenced to six years in prison for repeatedly raping a female resident with a disability in 2022."The violence women with disabilities experience is not an individual problem," Jo said. "It is structural violence, shaped by overlapping layers of gender, disability, institutionalisation, poverty and social isolation."'We want to live in peace'Since the case came to light, South Korea's prime minister has ordered the formation of a cross-government response team, calling the incident "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".In April, the government said it had inspected 1,507 residential facilities for disabled people nationwide and identified 33 suspected cases of abuse. So far investigations have been opened into eight of them.The government also said it would strengthen targeted inspections based on risk factors, as well as joint inspections involving local authorities, police and disability rights advocacy agencies.Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close and the local government has revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed. The local government has said it will draw up individual independent-living support plans for all 33 Saekdongwon residents. That process is still under way.Saekdongwon has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence. It has yet to comment on Kim's conviction.Asked what had changed most since leaving Saekdongwon, Seo said: "I just feel at peace. I'm happy every day."She also said the best thing was being able to eat and sleep when she wanted. What she wanted most now was "to cut ties with the director completely and never have anything to do with him again".But, Seo added, people with disabilities still need somewhere they could feel safe."I hope there can be a facility without sexual violence, where disabled people like us can live in peace."

schema.headline: The sexual abuse of disabled residents that shocked South Korea

title: NFL London: 'Money-grab' or celebration? London series begins amid anger over ticket prices
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Neither the Washington Commanders nor Indianapolis Colts qualified for last season's play-offsByBen CollinsBB
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Neither the Washington Commanders nor Indianapolis Colts qualified for last season's play-offsByBen CollinsBBC Sport journalist at Tottenham Hotspur StadiumOnce upon a time, tickets for NFL games in London were like gold dust.All 43 games have been near capacity at Wembley, Twickenham and Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.According to the NFL, its UK fanbase has swelled to 18.6 million, with 4.5 million of those considered 'avid' fans.So in the build-up to this year's London series, why were thousands of tickets still available for two of the three games?Next week's clash between the Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham sold out in hours.But the crowd for Sunday's game at Tottenham between Washington Commanders and Indianapolis Colts only reached 60,907 after ticket prices were slashed, and large sections remain unsold for the Wembley game on 18 October.The NFL is playing a record nine regular-season games abroad this season but 19 years after the first London game, has the NFL reached a saturation point in the UK?Why have ticket sales been slow?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Most of the fans BBC Sport spoke to at Sunday's game had travelled from the United StatesTickets to see Indianapolis beat Washington 30-13 on Sunday went on sale in July at £79-£245.But the NFL then dropped prices twice, in late August and again last week. That meant some fans who paid £185 were sat next to fans who paid £79 a few days ago.Some tickets were also discounted or free via the Blue Light Card and Tickets For Good platforms.Matt Cullen has travelled from Cambridge to most of the London games and said there were two main reasons for the slow sales; a price hike and a season-ticket package being scrapped."I find the prices now mind-boggling," he added. "It's so far above the rate of inflation that it just feels like a money-grab. It's priced out a lot of long-term fans."In 2019, tickets ranged from £55 to £125. According to Ticket-Compare,, external UK inflation has since risen by about 32.4% and the cheapest NFL London tickets have risen by 43.9%. The most expensive have seen a 96.5% hike.Season-ticket packages had been available, guaranteeing seats for each London game with a discount, but they were scrapped after the 2024 season."It felt like a kick to the head for a lot of loyal fans who'd supported the games for a long time and spent a lot of money," said Cullen, a former season-ticket holder. "But I do understand the NFL wants to bring new fans in."Why NFL expansion is a 'double-edged sword'UK fans have also complained about the quality of recent match-ups in London when compared to those in the new countries where the NFL has expanded.Australia hosted a divisional clash between the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams last month, while the Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys played out a thriller in Brazil last week."It was an amazing game and we haven't had many of those unfortunately," added Cullen.The best team coming to London this year is Philadelphia, who have reached two of the past four Super Bowls, and their game next week is a sell-out even though it was the most expensive.The Jaguars face the Houston Texans in two weeks and Dave, another former season-ticket holder, will travel from Chorley."We were all gutted when they took the season tickets away," he admitted. "The way we saw it, we weren't wanted anymore because we didn't spend the money that new fans do on merchandise and we get to the stadium later."But it has opened it up for more fans to have the opportunity to attend so it's a double-edged sword."'One of the greatest events for neutrals'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jonathan Taylor ran in two touchdowns as the Colts beat the Commanders and produced a tea-sipping celebrationBBC Sport spoke to dozens of fans at Sunday's game and none of them were aware ticket prices had dropped. None seemed to care either.American fans know the London games don't provide the same tailgating experience they get back home, but they - and the players - are still fascinated by the eclectic crowd at international games.Fans still travel from all over the UK, Europe and the US, wearing jerseys of all the NFL teams."It's still one of the greatest sporting events that neutrals can go to," said Dave. "I don't think there's any other sport where you'd get tens of thousands watching teams they don't support."It was always a celebration of the game. People would go for the love of the sport rather than the two teams that were playing and I think that's still the same."It sure felt like a Washington home game when they recovered a Colts fumble on just the game's second play.The crowd produced an even bigger roar when third-choice quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis - replacing the injured Marcus Mariota - made a 47-yard touchdown pass to Treylon Burks in the third quarter.The Commanders thought they had drawn level when Antonio Williams ran in an 87-yard score, but the touchdown was chalked off for a Washington penalty.Indianapolis quarterback Daniel Jones then got in to seal their success, with Jonathan Taylor having run in two touchdowns for the Colts.Biles sprinkles stardust on London openerImage source, NFL/APImage caption, Simone Biles wore a customised outfit bearing her husband's name and numberIt is hard to imagine anyone went home disappointed, no matter what price they paid.The stands were bathed in sunshine and fans looked like they were having the time of their life as they sang Sweet Caroline and Wonderwall in unison.Oasis' Noel Gallagher was booed when he appeared on the big screen - no doubt because of his football allegiance to Manchester City - and former Manchester United and England striker Wayne Rooney was also among the crowd, wearing a half-and-half scarf.Olympian Simone Biles travelled to London to support her husband Jonathan Owens, who is a safety for the Colts, and as long as stars such as those show up at NFL games, international fans will want to be there too."There's been a lot of anger from fans on social media about the ticket prices but it's only what they do with last-minute holidays," added Dave."Even though some of us fans see it as poor way for the NFL to run it, they've got a full stadium."We're just not used to dynamic pricing in the UK. It was the same with Oasis tickets for their reunion. We were outraged at that but we still all went didn't we."

schema.headline: NFL London: 'Money-grab' or celebration? London series begins amid anger over ticket prices

title: The job interview question you don't have to answer
description: When interviewing or deciding on new staff, employers must not discriminate against an applicant based on so-called protected characteristics, includi
body: When interviewing or deciding on new staff, employers must not discriminate against an applicant based on so-called protected characteristics, including age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation.Sometimes it feels like interviewers, and interviewees, tip-toe around the subject of money.But Louise Rudd, a senior adviser at the workplace advice and conciliation service Acas, says there are no regulations that prevent employers from asking interviewees about their current salary, or their salary expectations.She says employers, if they do want to know, should ask each applicant the same questions to ensure they are treated fairly.A few years ago, a campaign was launched urging employers to stop asking new recruits how much they were paid in their previous jobs. It had its own hashtag - #EndSalaryHistory.The Fawcett Society, which campaigns for women and gender equality, said that asking the question risked maintaining historic unfair differences in pay due to gender, race and disability inequality. Rather than offering a salary based on skills, experience and performance, it meant employers rewarded an individual's perceived worth and negotiating skills instead, the society said.When you're going for a new job, you can reveal your current salary if you are happy to.Some people asked by BBC News out and about in London suggested they would reply with an inflated salary - so they get paid more in the next job. However, the risks of lying in an interview can far outweigh the possible reward.There are no requirements for you to disclose your salary if you don't want to.Rudd says some people might prefer to give their salary expectations, or outline their understanding of the salary range for the role.Recruitment firms often say applicants could instead focus on their skills and experience, so those are used as a measure of what they should be paid, not their salary history. Shazia Ejaz, director of campaigns at the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, says jobseekers should approach questions about pay with "realism but also confidence". "Candidates can focus on showcasing the value they bring, the benefits that matter most to them and to go to the interview knowing the market rate for the role," she says."Jobseekers who have done their homework on salaries and can explain the contribution they will make are in the strongest position to secure the right package."

schema.headline: The job interview question you don't have to answer

title: Arsenal are 10 points off WSL leaders Man City - is Renee Slegers' job at risk?
description: It is only five matches into the Women's Super League season and Arsenal are already 10 points behind leaders Manchester City - so is manager Renee Sl
body: It is only five matches into the Women's Super League season and Arsenal are already 10 points behind leaders Manchester City - so is manager Renee Slegers' position at risk?The Gunners have won just two of their opening seven matches in all competitions and sit 10th in the WSL table. It is dismal reading for Arsenal fans, whose optimism has quickly diminished and their 4-2 defeat at City on Sunday added further salt to their wounds.The Gunners have not won a WSL title since 2019 and it has been a familiar story each year as slow starts have ultimately proven costly.Slegers did lead Arsenal to the Women's Champions League title in 2025. But they failed to win any domestic trophies last season, although they did finish second in the WSL and reached the semi-finals in the defence of their European crown.Asked if she was worried about her position, Slegers said: "All I know so far is that the last couple of days we have been together as a club, and a team."We have been aligned in the direction. Of course, this result is disappointing but I'm here and I'm full of energy. I care a lot for the club and the players. I see perspective."It's good to have an international break coming up. It's good for the players to change environment, play their football elsewhere, then come back in with new energy."At full-time on Sunday, Slegers gathered her dejected players in a familiar team huddle before walking over to their fans.She stood in front of the 2,500 away supporters at Etihad Stadium applauding as they sang "North London Forever" in a somewhat emotional release. She was greeted warmly and it did not look like a fanbase who were keen to push her out of the door.Arsenal had performed reasonably well against City, took the lead twice and were ultimately undone by small margins. "I mostly went there to thank them, connect with them and show them I care for them and I appreciate them coming out to Manchester," said Slegers. "I also wanted to show that – not that I feel sorry for them as I'm a big part of it too – but they are coming here and not getting the rewards, just like the team. "I just wanted to connect with them instead of walking away and hiding. I don't know how they are going to react to me! I just wanted to thank them for being there for us."Outside of the stadium however, noise among the fanbase has been building and Slegers knows her position is being questioned.Sources at the club insist she retains their full backing and, while there is disappointment and acknowledgement that results have not been good enough, they believe Slegers can guide them in the right direction. There was investment in the transfer window with the likes of England international Georgia Stanway and Spain full-back Ona Batlle arriving, as well as the talented, young Germany forward Lisa Baum.Those signings were made early in an attempt to ensure a full pre-season and avoid a slow start with most players returning to Arsenal from their holidays in mid-July.It has clearly not paid off but rather than worry about her job, Slegers is already planning an inquest into where the problems lie during the international break."There will be a big review of our season so far," she added, when asked if there was a wider club issue regarding their continuous slow starts to WSL seasons.Some of the issues have been obvious. They had scored just twice in the WSL prior to Sunday's match and Alessia Russo's goal in the 49th minute against City was her first in the league this season.That lack of ruthlessness has meant Arsenal have failed to win in their past four WSL games - their worst winless streak since October 2023.Defeat by City also confirmed this as their second-worst start after five games in the WSL, only picking up fewer points (four) in 2014.Confidence has clearly taken a hit and Wednesday's bizarre error from defender Leah Williamson summed up the chaotic nature of their season so far.Emotions were high after their 2-2 draw with Paris FC in the Women's Champions League, so much so that Slegers did not show up for post-match media duties.She later explained her actions, saying she was angry and felt the team needed her in that moment. But despite the obvious concerns for Arsenal, Slegers was defiant on Sunday, stating she believes she remains the right person to lead the club."First of all, it's not about me anyway. I have energy, I feel the connection and I think we're going through a really difficult time but we also see perspective," she said. "We look forward and see solutions. We see the closeness [of the squad]. It's not that we're totally away from it or off it, it's been consistently about margins. "We have to work to get them on our side but when we do, I think we'll be really good. Of course, it's been a long run without the results we wanted. "It's not about me, it's about the club and I care about the club."

schema.headline: Arsenal are 10 points off WSL leaders Man City - is Renee Slegers' job at risk?

title: Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Lewis Hamilton bemused after F1 'Lego race'
description: Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton likened the effects of a software bug that affected multiple cars before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to a "Le
body: Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton likened the effects of a software bug that affected multiple cars before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to a "Lego race".The problem led to several cars, including those of the two multiple world champions who were sharing the front row of the grid, not working in the wet conditions that preceded the race.A tropical downpour delayed attempts to get the grand prix under way for the best part of an hour. And when the cars set off on formation laps behind a safety car to test the conditions, audiences were treated to the bizarre sight of many of them struggling to move.A bug in the software that mandates how the engines' electrical power can be used in wet conditions had been triggered by a combination of low engine speeds, low grip and specific aspects of the circuit layout.Verstappen, who went on to take a dominant win that was his first victory of the year, said: "These engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented."I triggered [the problem] first and then I looked in my mirror, I was like, 'Wait, are they waiting for me or what's going [on]...?' It was like the Lego race."Verstappen was referring to a show run in battery-powered Lego F1 cars that was held before the British Grand Prix in July.Hamilton, sitting beside Verstappen in the post-race news conference after finishing third, interjected to say: "Yeah, we had the same speed. I had to stop on track and stop the car and engine and restart it. I've never done that before."Verstappen added: "It was insane. Like, it's the Lego power. At some point we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on. "Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still, and I saw you (Hamilton) by yourself crawling. That's not what you want, right, for the sport."Mercedes driver George Russell, who retired from the race with an engine failure, said: "It didn't feel very F1." Nikolas Tombazis, the single-seater director for governing body the FIA said there would be a full investigation.The issue arose, he added, because, while the software had been tested, it had not been tested in these specific conditions. Largely because there has been so little running in the wet this year."Cars are complicated," Tombazis said. "We would all like it to be simpler, but when you have electrical energy and combustion energy all working together, and obviously when you want to ensure that there's sporting fairness between the teams, that is complicated."We haven't done a full debrief of the situation and see how we can avoid such an issue. Every race, we have a long debrief afterwards, where we identify criticalities."Obviously, that was a major criticality, and we need to make sure we avoid it. Can I guarantee it will never happen again? This specific problem, yes. A problem, no, but we will do our best to avoid it, of course."This is far from the first issue created by the huge complexity of the latest hybrid engines introduced this year, with their near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power.Because the engines are fundamentally energy starved, and so cannot deploy their full combined power output at all times, a series of complexities were added into the management of the engines to try to sticking-plaster solutions.Many of these led to the counter-intuitive driving about which many of the sport's stars have been complaining all season - and more changes have been added since.Off-track conversation has been dominated by this all year, and rules are changing for next year to alter the energy split to try to ameliorate the issue.McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "What happened at the start obviously is not ideal in terms of presentation of the sport."But at the same time it is the first year of new regulations, quite complex from a regulatory point of view, and it was also the first time we started in such conditions."So we have to concede that F1 has done an excellent job in making some new regulations that came with some question marks from a power-unit behaviour point of view when it came to racing for instance."We have to acknowledge there has been really good work to make the show and racing work, and if there are some glitches occasionally, we have to accept they are glitches for everyone, be supportive and make sure it doesn't happen again."The problem had a secondary consequence - the field order was jumbled up, and one reading of the rules could have meant the grid order should change for any restart.But while the FIA's software engineers were rewriting the code as fast as possible, it was determined that, as this situation had never occurred before, and as the problem was out of any competitor's control, the most appropriate order was to revert to the original grid.Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "If you think of the millions of people watching around the world, they tune in for the start and suddenly the cars are all in a jumbled up order because of something that happened 40 minutes earlier and it was behind a safety car on a formation lap. That would have been a much harder thing to explain than resetting and then going from where we did."Verstappen's 'amazing' win crowns Red Bull comeback"Amazing" was the word Verstappen chose to describe his and Red Bull's first win of the 2026 season at a chaotic, bizarre and, in some ways, unprecedented race.It would be wrong to say the victory was a complete surprise, as it came after three consecutive podium finishes in which the four-time champion appeared to be edging closer and closer to such an achievement.But it certainly adds a fresh twist to a season of fluctuating fortunes at the front, in which the only real constant has been Kimi Antonelli, as the championship heads into its final stretch.It was Verstappen's 72nd victory and it came in a manner entirely familiar to those who have followed his career - but entirely unfamiliar to this season.The Dutchman was the man all weekend at Sepang, where Verstappen also won the last time the track held a race in 2017. As early as Friday afternoon his rivals were all saying he was going to be difficult to beat.He duly delivered a dominant win, which barely looked in doubt even through the chaos of a delayed start, software glitches caused by a bug in the mandated FIA engine settings that wreaked havoc for him and several other drivers on a formation lap, losing the lead to the two Mercedes off the line and a late safety car period.What was remarkable about that, though, is that until Malaysia not once so far this season had Verstappen had been in this position.Red Bull started this year in a bit of a state.The fourth fastest car among the big four teams, it was debatable at times in the early races whether their car was even better than that of their junior team, Racing Bulls.All year, Verstappen has been battling an inconsistent handling balance and there was doubt for some time as to whether he would even stay at Red Bull beyond this year.Although contracted until the end of 2028, it was widely known there were performance-related clauses in his contract that allowed him to leave, and McLaren courted him in the summer.In the end, though. Verstappen decided to stay, saying he liked the environment at Red Bull, he had faith they would return to the front, and he did not mind a bit of extra work helping them do it.Those sentiments were expressed in an interview at the Italian Grand Prix a month ago. He finished third that weekend, but even that recently there was no indication a performance such as this was in the offing.But a trickle of upgrades in the past few races finally all came together with the introduction of a new floor in Baku, the weekend before Malaysia.There, awkward circumstances in qualifying left him eighth on the grid when by merit he would have been on the front row. But a late safety car closed up the field, and he spent the final stint right on the gearbox of George Russell's leading Mercedes, and lost out on the win by less than 0.2secs.Malaysia proved that promise was more than a flash in the pan."We had a very complicated and tough start to the year with all sorts of problems and just not being competitive enough,' Verstappen said on Sunday."But throughout the year, the team has been working very hard to understand our issues and bring good performance upgrades to the car and make it more driveable."Step by step, we've been getting closer and closer, and today, and of course especially this whole weekend, we've been really in good form. So, yeah, it's amazing."There are six or seven races remaining, depending on whether F1 gets the security reassurances it needs to give it the final confidence to commit to the end of the season grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi in the context of the war in the Middle East.On this basis, Verstappen could well be a factor in all of them.If the championship battle had any jeopardy remaining in it, that would certainly up the ante. But Russell's retirement from third place with an engine failure with five laps to go in Malaysia has pretty much eradicated that.Antonelli's second place and Russell's retirement extended the Italian's lead to 84 points. With either 158 or 183 remaining in total, depending on how the season ends, that size of lead means only some kind of miraculous turn of events could turn the tide back in Russell's favour.He said: "I don't need to say I think it's gone, but, of course, it's exceptionally unlikely and that's just the reality."I knew if I wanted to come back, I needed luck on my side. Unfortunately, I had luck not on my side."So, you know, a three-point loss today being behind Kimi turned into an 18-point loss. Of course, if it was on the other side it would have been an 18-point gain. So it's a real shame, but that's just how it is."It's not the first time an engine problem has robbed Russell of big points this year. But Antonelli has had his reliability issues, too, and to about the same level.The reality is that Antonelli has been the better performer this year - as he was again in Malaysia after his odd off weekend in Baku - and he will deserve the title when it comes.Russell 'beyond disappointment'If the championship battle had any jeopardy remaining in it, that would certainly up the ante. But Russell's retirement from third place with an engine failure with five laps to go in Malaysia has pretty much eradicated that.Antonelli's second place and Russell's retirement extended the Italian's lead to 84 points. With either 158 or 183 remaining in total, depending on how the season ends, that size of lead means only some kind of miraculous turn of events could turn the tide back in Russell's favour."I don't need to say I think it's gone," Russell said, "but, of course, it's exceptionally unlikely and that's just the reality."I knew if I wanted to come back, I needed luck on my side. Unfortunately, I had luck not on my side."So, you know, a three-point loss today being behind Kimi turned into an 18-point loss. Of course, if it was on the other side it would have been an 18-point gain. So it's a real shame, but that's just how it is."It's not the first time an engine problem has robbed Russell of big points this year. "You've almost got to laugh," he said. "I'm beyond disappointment. It's just so many times this season it's happened. It's a real shame. Of course, but just keep on fighting."But Antonelli has had his reliability issues, too, and to about the same level.The reality, as Russell has acknowledged many times, is that Antonelli has been the better performer on balance this year - as he was again in Malaysia after his off weekend in Baku - and he will deserve the title when it comes.

schema.headline: Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Lewis Hamilton bemused after F1 'Lego race'

title: Girl, 12, fatally shot in US during 'dispute over parking space'
description: A 12-year-old girl was killed in Baltimore over the weekend during an apparent disagreement over a parking space, police in the US city said. The girl
body: A 12-year-old girl was killed in Baltimore over the weekend during an apparent disagreement over a parking space, police in the US city said. The girl was caught in the crossfire of bullets between two men who police said were allegedly fighting over a parking space in a park where children were playing American football.In addition to the young girl, a woman was also found with gunshot wounds when police arrived on the scene. Two men also visited area hospitals for injuries believed to be related to the shooting, police said.Police are now searching for at least two suspects, Baltimore Police Commissioner Richard Worley said at a news conference. No arrests have been made."What we know is there was some type of argument between two cowards," Worley said. "They both opened fire on each other. In the crossfire, a 12-year-old little girl, who was probably down there watching football, was shot and killed."Worley said the girl, who police have not named, was not a target of the shooting.The girl was pronounced dead in hospital. The other three individuals who were injured have non-life-threatening injuries, Worley said.The incident happened after 18:00 EDT (23:00 BST) on Saturday.Authorities are still investigating the shooting and have asked any witnesses to bring information to police. It remains unclear how many shots were fired, Worley said. "Two grown men got into an argument, and now a 12-year-old is gone," Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott said at the news conference. "We never should have to say something like that. What happened out here today is one of the most disgusting things I've ever seen in my life."

schema.headline: Girl, 12, fatally shot in US during 'dispute over parking space'

title: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
description: Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and
body: Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and a 100 page statement on her guiding principles., external"I believe in common sense, people working hard and being rewarded for that effort," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.She added that welfare should be a "safety net, not a lifestyle".The Tory leader is trying to ensure her party stands out in a crowded political field. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in the opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, has characterised Reform leader Nigel Farage as a "grumpy grandpa" and she told Laura Kuenssberg that Labour leader Andy Burnham is "the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes".She described herself as a "no-nonsense mum".Asked if her plan for benefit cuts and a massive increase in prison places was a return to the "nasty party" of the past, she said: "It's the common sense party. That's what we're doing."And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?"In her essay The Right Way - a deliberate echo of an essay written by Margaret Thatcher in 1976, external entitled The Right Approach - Badenoch says the last Conservative government failed because it did not know what it stood for.Despite the party's rhetoric during its 14 years in power, she said: "We did little to reverse the structural changes Labour had made which took the country in the wrong direction. "The result was that the state grew by stealth."The essay says the "next Conservative government will have one central principle: business, not government, creates growth".The Tories would achieve growth through tax cuts, cutting red tape and reducing the size of the civil service back to pre-pandemic levels, the essay says.And it adds: "What is really missing from politics and government today is people prepared to say no. "Political parties now need to recruit those who have the stomach to say no to good causes when the resources simply are not there to do everything."As their conference gets under way in Birmingham the Conservatives have pledged to end a childcare "cliff edge", which currently means parents earning more than £100,000 do not qualify for the entitlement.The party has also promised to deliver 50,000 new prison places by slashing the overseas aid budget to £1bn a year in a bid to end the early release of offenders.Over the 14 years the Conservatives were in power, around 500 net prison places were created, which takes into account 14,142 added in existing and new jails, set against 13,660 lost mainly to dilapidation and closures.Speaking in the main conference hall, Badenoch sought to make the case that the party had moved on from 2024 and outlined her expectation that the next few days in Birmingham would be a chance for members to discuss their ideas.She said: "We're going to be having debates, we're going to have arguments, they are going to be fun."We're going to challenge each other and afterwards we're still going to be a united party."During a question and answer session, Badenoch focused on different topics covered in her essay – including citizenship and how communities need to operate on trust.She said the UK is "not a dormitory, it is not a hotel" before speaking how "British culture means something".To applause in the well-attended hall, Badenoch said: "I don't want lots of little ghettos of separatist communities where they are recreating the place they come from - that will ruin the United Kingdom."Responding, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said the Tory Party "is stuck in the past and remains completely out of touch with what people across Britain want to see"."Last week Andy Burnham set out a plan to bring back hope to Britain. Kemi Badenoch wants to drag our country back to a politics that let so many people down over the past 40 years."

schema.headline: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch

title: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' conference motion
description: Israel's foreign ministry says it has banned Green Party leader Zack Polanski from entering the country, after party members adopted a motion declarin
body: Israel's foreign ministry says it has banned Green Party leader Zack Polanski from entering the country, after party members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.Israel's foreign ministry described the motion as a "clear antisemitic text" and beyond "the boundaries of legitimate political debate".Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday. The motion, which has has divided senior party figures, defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".It has been criticised by some Jewish groups, who called the motion an "attack on the Jewish community"."Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it," the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council  said in a statement."Branding most British Jews and Jewish institutions 'racist' stokes anti-Jewish hatred after a year in which British Jews have been murdered attending their synagogue, stabbed in the streets, and seen their community buildings firebombed."Israel's foreign ministry said the motion was "a stain on the history of the United Kingdom".The party's joint deputy leaders have been at odds over the subject, with Mothin Ali backing the move, and Rachel Millward describing the wording as "problematic".But members endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813."The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it says.Discussion about the vote has dominated the conference, and exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general  election. Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression"."We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added. Polanski did not vote in the debate, having left the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a by-election to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here. Asked about the motion on Friday, Polanski said: "If your Zionism is the displacement of the Palestinian people then that is clearly racist, and I say that as a Jewish leader of a British political party."However, he said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like."He had also said he wanted to see the motion amended to specify that it should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.However, both amendments favoured by Polanski were rejected by Green members.The Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council statement referred to a "particular criticism" for Polanski "who neither spoke against the motion nor voted" but welcomed the subsequent "cross-party condemnation".A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist.Speaking after the motion had been approved, Vivien Lichtenstein, chairwoman of Jewish Greens,  told the BBC she could consider her future in the party. Polanski has not specified whether he supports the motion passed by members, but added his name to a joint statement from the party's five MPs and deputy leaders issued after the vote.The statement pledged to ensure the Green Party was "an anti-racist party in every way" and added that there was "no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people".Over the course of the three-day conference, key figures in the party have expressed differing positions about the Zionism motion. Four of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer, Sian Berry - had publicly opposed it, with Denyer arguing it could risk "alienating a significant proportion of Jewish people".Chowns, as well as former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas, both spoke against the motion during the debate.Addressing members, Lucas said: "I urge you not to support the over-simplification at the heart of this motion - a refusal to accept complexities which is leading to so many Jewish members feeling scared and unwelcome in our party."Deputy leader Mothin Ali, who had expressed support for the motion before the vote, said it was calling for "a state that's democratic, that guarantees the rights of every single person living on that land".He added that he was "absolutely not" calling all Jewish people who define themselves as Zionists racist.Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election. The Conservatives criticised the motion, saying it demonstrated the Green Party was "toxic to its core". Labour chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said the vote "crosses a line" and called on Polanski to "make clear that this will not be their position moving forwards"."It is shameful to vote against a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine and to condemn the vast majority of British Jews and Jews around the world as racist for supporting Israel's right to exist," she added.Liberal Democrat MP Luke Taylor said the motion did not address "the rising threats" of Islamophobia and antisemitism in the UK.He added: "This is a divisive motion that pours fuel on the fire of tensions in the UK, and will leave many British Jews feeling less safe."

schema.headline: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' conference motion

title: Andrew Griffith to unveil Tory plans to cut taxes and regulations
description: Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith is to outline his plans for the UK economy, including hopes to cut taxes, red tape and house-building c
body: Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith is to outline his plans for the UK economy, including hopes to cut taxes, red tape and house-building costs.Griffith and his colleagues will use day two of the party's conference in Birmingham to also explain how they would want to reduce food costs, support Heathrow Airport expansion and abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency. Another prospective policy is replacing agreements designed to compel developers to fund community projects and services in areas they want to build.Griffith will describe his approach as the "most ambitious deregulation project in a generation". Reform UK suggested the Tories were "copying our policies".Griffith's speech comes after Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch published a 100-page document, external explaining her guiding principles and how her party would act should it return to government by winning the next general election.Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again.The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government, including on the economy, between 2010 and 2024. Griffith is expected to say: "No-one else is coming to save our economy.  Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation."He will accuse Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to pursue a "socialist fever dream of the 1970s", adding the Tories want to deliver "cheaper homes, lower taxes, and less red tape".Chancellor John Healey last week said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".During a series of speeches on Monday, Conservative shadow ministers will continue to make their case and provide more details of their proposals.This will include ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, including the future homes standard. The Tories believe their changes could cut the cost of delivering a new home by up to £50,000, which in turn they expect could save money for buyers.A single levy for developers would be implemented in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed.The Conservatives argue this new charge would remove delays and improve how the funds are spent to the benefit of residents.The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would also be scrapped by the Conservatives.The party believes this would help lift a "burden" from businesses and in turn could cut the cost of the weekly shop.On Heathrow, Griffith is expected to say the next Conservative government would do "whatever it takes to end the delays and boost capacity by backing the third runway".Plans for expansion were scrapped by the Tory-led coalition government in 2010.Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves championed the runway to boost the economy after Labour won power, although Burnham has refused to say whether he backs the project since becoming prime minister.Burnham has described it as "principally... a matter for London and Londoners".Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the Conservatives have "cemented their position as a pointless anti-growth anti-business party" by rejecting closer ties with Europe.She added: "No-one can take anything the Conservatives say on the economy seriously given their litany of fantasy-land financial pledges."Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick accused the Conservatives of "once again copying our policies". He added the Tories were unable to match Reform's pledge to raise the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.
